en: The *Sūtra on the Ritual Procedures for the Colors and Forms of the Lotus Sūtra Maṇḍala*,
which establishes the wondrous Dharma: from within a precious stūpa emerging atop an eight-petaled lotus flower of the *Lotus Sūtra King*,
there appear the two-footed Bhagavān and the eight great bodhisattvas, along with the three-tiered square altar.

The Sutra on the Method for Accomplishing the Eightfold Great Assembly of Equality, the Maṇḍala of Māyā’s Retinue with Their Sublime Dignity, Form, and Color; the Assembly for Fulfilling Vows, the Directions, and the Symbols; the Flower-Samādhi of Manifestation in the Present Life, Entering the First Stage, and the Definitive Realization of Bodhi, flowing forth from the Blue Stream.
Translated by Amoghavajra, the Great Sage of Wide Wisdom, at Daxingshan Temple in the Central Capital, by Imperial Decree.
At that time, Vairocana Bhagavān addressed the Bodhisattva Guhyapāṇi-vajradhara, saying:

O Son of the Buddha, listen with a sincere mind to the exposition of the characteristics of the Great Maṇḍala of the Sublime Dharma that brings fulfillment, the positions of the various deities in the Assembly for the Fulfillment of Vows, and even the rules concerning their majestic deportment, physical forms, and colors.
This is what is called the inner maṇḍala.
That very ground of the body is the self-nature of the dharmadhātu;
it is empowered by the empowerment of mantras and secret mudrās.
Its intrinsic nature is pure,
for it is protected and sustained by the four great vajras; thus,
all defilements and impurities are completely cleansed away.
The afflictions of the notions of self, person, sentient being, life-span, mind-born, youth, and a mere stump;
the ground of deep blue lapis lazuli and the golden boundary-mandala;
and exquisite lotus flowers scattered everywhere upon it.
The square altar faces west at its entrance and extends throughout the surrounding boundary paths;
within it appears the eight-petaled Flower King born of mind,
with a stem of *yū* and spreading blossoms.
The overall design is exquisite and subtle;
it is as fresh and white as snow,
emitting a pure, radiant luster.
Its color transcends that of the world;
between its petals are three golden rings,
upon the calyx of the flower.
There emerged great stūpas made of the seven treasures,
five hundred yojanas in height and equally wide and broad,
each measuring three hundred and fifty yojanas.
Upon that pavilion dwells the wish-fulfilling gem,
surrounded by a wreath of flames.
It is adorned with the "Golden Locks of Zhang" and precious bells suspended everywhere,
embellished with various kinds of rare treasures.
There were five thousand railings and ten million niches,
with countless banners suspended from them.
It was adorned with necklaces of the seven precious gems,
and five-precious bells and chimes hung down from it.
From all four sides, the fragrance of *tamālapatra* sandalwood issued forth.
Throughout the great trichiliocosm,
the heavens rained down precious flowers,
which fell in profusion as an offering.
At that time, within the stupa, upon the lion throne,
the two-footed Holy Honored Ones, Śākyamuni and Prabhūtaratna,
sat half-cross-legged and half-seated.
Each sits together upon an eight-petaled lotus flower;
these are the eight great bodhisattvas.
The most honored and extraordinary body among all worlds,
transcending body, speech, and mind,
reaches the ground of the mind where it attains a distinction that surpasses the realm of the intellect.
On the eight petals, beginning from the northeast corner and proceeding clockwise,
the eight great bodhisattvas are arranged:
first, Maitreya Bodhisattva.
Next were Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva,
Bhaiṣajyarāja Bodhisattva,
and Gadgadasvara Bodhisattva.
The Bodhisattva Constantly Diligent,
the Bodhisattva Inexhaustible Intent,
and the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara.
Samantabhadra Bodhisattva.
Within the four corners of this inner courtyard,
first, at the northeast corner, is Mahākāśyapa.
In the southeast was Subhūti;
in the southwest, Śāriputra;
and in the northwest, Mahāmaudgalyāyana.
Next, in the second courtyard,
place the Bodhisattva Vajraśṛṅkhala at the eastern gate and the Bodhisattva Vajraghaṇṭā at the southern gate.
The Bodhisattva Vajrāṅkuśa is positioned before the stūpa;
the Bodhisattva Vajrapāśa is at the northern gate;
and the Bodhisattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta is placed to the north of the eastern gate.
At the southern gate, place the Bodhisattva Ratnapāṇi.
Next, at the eastern side of the southern gate, place the Bodhisattva Ratnaketu.
At the western side of the gate, place the Bodhisattva Jyotirāja.
Next, place the Bodhisattva Ratnacandra to the south of the western gate,
and the Bodhisattva Pūrṇacandra to the north.
Next, place the Bodhisattva Śūradatta to the west of the northern gate.
To the east, place the Bodhisattva Sarvavidhi-siddhi;
furthermore, within the northeast corner, place the Bodhisattva Puṣpārcana;
and in the southeast corner, the Bodhisattva Dīpārcana.
In the southwest corner, place the Bodhisattva Gandhapūjā;
in the northwest corner, offer worship to the Bodhisattva Dhūpapūjā.
Next, in the third tiered enclosure:
The Heavenly King Dhṛtarāṣṭra is stationed at the eastern gate;
the Heavenly King Virūḍhaka is stationed at the southern gate;
and the Heavenly King Virūpākṣa is stationed at the western gate.
The Great Brahmā Deva King is placed at the north gate;
Śakra Devendra is placed to the south of the gate;
and Maheśvara is placed to the east of the south gate.
At the western gate, place the Nāga King Nanda.
To the south of the western gate, place the Yakṣa King Sudharmasundara.
To the north of the gate, place the Gandharva King Rativādī.
To the west of the northern gate, place Rāhu, the Asura King;
to the east of the gate, place Māṇibhadra, the Garuḍa King;
and in the northeast corner, the noble Ucchuṣma Vajra.
In the southeastern corner, place the noble Vajra Cunda;
in the southwestern corner, place the noble Vajra Acala;
and in the northwestern corner, place the noble Vajra Trailokyavijaya.
On the four sides of the maṇḍala,
draw the boundary lines for food and drink,
and also draw the four gates.
Upon the altar, a celestial canopy was spread,
and twenty-four banners were suspended on its four sides.
Furthermore, at each of the four corners,
erect banners and streamers, and four auspicious jars (*kalaśa*) with black bases,
filled to the brim with scented water.
Insert fresh and exquisite flowers into the mouth of the vase.
At both sides of the four gates of the maṇḍala, [place them].
Place two arghya vessels, each filled with scented water and containing saffron,
in their respective positions.
They scattered various seasonal flowers throughout,
making it exceedingly fragrant and pure.
Furthermore, at the four gates, they...
Place four incense burners and burn five-flavored incense to make offerings.
Furthermore, at each of its four corners,
place a copper lampstand,
with ghee and oil serving as the light.
At the four corners outside,
drive in stakes of khadira wood;
if this wood is unavailable, [use another].
It is also permissible to cast copper into the form of a stake as a substitute.
This concludes the *Sādhana-vidhi for the Yoga-contemplative Wisdom of the King of the Lotus Sūtra*,
which explains the majestic deportment, physical appearance, and the orientation of a single mudrā.
Having already explained the ritual procedures within the maṇḍala and the characteristics of the adornment of the single-tiered precious stūpa,
I shall now describe the majestic deportment, physical form, and color of the two principal deities within the stūpa.
With a crown of deep blue hair and the *ūrṇā* tuft between the brows emitting light that illuminates all,
his body is the color of golden-yellow; he forms the mudrā of concentration,
wisdom, and knowledge, seated in the full lotus posture with the right foot over the left.
With the left spoke of his wheel hanging down, his body clad in the robes of a monk,
he dwells upon a great lotus flower; constantly traversing the full moon disk,
his radiance pervades everywhere as he emerges from within a jeweled stupa.
He has realized the sublime Wheel of Dharma, which he causes to turn perpetually without interruption;
his hair is as dark as refined oil or deep indigo, and the white tuft between his brows radiates light toward the east for eighty thousand leagues; his physical form is the color of gold.
The left hand forms the fist seal of firm resolve; the right hand, representing wisdom, opens outward with the square shape,
bending the ring finger (of ignorance) and the little finger (of minor delusion), while the middle and index fingers (the head) are aligned,
sitting in the cross-legged posture with the left leg pressing upon the right, and the wheel of the right spoke hanging downward.
Clad in the robes of the kashaya, dwelling securely upon white lotuses,
and constantly roaming within the lunar disc,
his brilliance blazes forth in splendor so that the Teaching may spread; abiding therein, he expounds the Dharma.
Surrounded by a multitude of samādhis, each holding a sūtra—
having already explained the physical characteristics (*rūpalakṣaṇa*) of the two bodies of the Tathāgata,
[the text] now explains the marks and signs (*lakṣaṇavyañjana*) of the eight great bodhisattvas.
The king of the eight-petaled lotus begins from the petal in the northeast corner and proceeds clockwise,
with Maitreya at its head;
he wears a sublime jewel crown upon his head, and his deep blue hair hangs down over both shoulders.
The physical form is also the color of flesh; in the left hand is a purple lotus in the mudrā of concentration, upon which he holds a bell.

In the right hand is the mudrā of wisdom, massaging the knee, seated in the full lotus posture with the right foot pressing upon the left. This is the embodiment of Great Loving-kindness and Great Compassion.
His body is clad in the saffron-colored robe; with pearl garlands, precious necklaces, and bracelets of jade for his arms;
with exquisite celestial garments of a thousand colors, fine and soft, and a wondrous lower garment of vermilion red.
His body is adorned with the marks and signs of excellence;
he possesses the three eyes and the radiance of twelve moons, with a conch-shell complexion.
His light pervades everywhere, and he sits upon a supreme lotus seat within a great lunar disc.
Wearing a crown of five locks upon his head, with dark blue hair hanging down to his eyebrows;
his body is the color of golden light. His left hand holds a blue lotus, upon which rest three swords;
he sits in the full-lotus posture with the right leg placed over the left.
The aspect of compassionately welcoming and guiding: His body is draped in the robes of a monk, adorned with exquisite flower garlands and fine necklaces;
Bracelets and rings adorn his arms, and he wears subtle jade and wondrous celestial garments; A silken sash is fastened around his waist.
He wears robes of crimson radiance, his sublime body adorned with exquisite ornaments;
the light from his body is like an autumn rainbow.
He sits upon a seat of precious flowers, wearing a sublime jewel crown upon his head, with deep blue hair falling down by his ears.
The physical form has the color of the morning sun; the left hand forms the mudrā of stability resting on the knee, while the right hand holds a cloud of compassion above the sun.
Seated in the paryaṅka posture with the right leg over the left, he displays the aspect of Great Compassion that rescues the world, his body adorned with exquisite flower garlands.
Celestial robes and necklaces, bracelets and armlets of jade,
fine brocade for the waist, and scarlet silk for exquisite garments adorn his wondrous body;
the radiance of his body shines forth everywhere.
Seated upon a precious lotus, he dwells peacefully atop a moon disc and an ocean of jewels;
wearing a great precious crown, his deep blue hair hangs down to his ears, and his body is crimson-yellow in hue;
his left hand holds a lotus bud that has not yet opened.

With his right hand in the gesture of granting blessings and pressing upon his knee, he sits in the full lotus posture with the right leg over the left, manifesting the compassionate aspect of the Savior of the World.
His hair is adorned with flowers and necklaces, and he wears a fine celestial robe and a monastic saffron garment; his arms are decorated with jade bracelets.
A sash of ten thousand colors encircles the waist; He wears a lower garment the color of *bimba* fruit.
Adorned with a body of myriad virtues, His bodily radiance pervades all things.
With a lotus flower as his seat, He dwells peacefully within a full moon disc.
Wearing a sublime jewel crown upon his head, with deep blue hair hanging down to both ears;

his body is the color of white flesh; his left hand rests in the gesture of meditative concentration (dhyāna-mudrā) upon his knee, while his right holds a mani-jewel in the gesture of generosity (varada-mudrā);
he sits in the full lotus posture with the right leg pressing upon the left.
Compassionate toward all forms, adorned with pearl garlands, celestial robes,
and exquisite necklaces; wearing rare jade bracelets and a sash of fine silk,
he is clothed in garments of deep crimson.
His body is adorned with a hundred merits; a halo surrounds him like a blazing gem.
He sits upon a lotus throne made of jewels, dwelling peacefully within a lunar palace.
His exquisite crown adorns his five locks of hair, and his deep blue tresses hang down over both shoulders.
The physical form is the color of raw flesh; the left hand holds a lotus garland in the gesture of concentration, while the right forms a fist of wisdom resting upon the knee.
Seated in the full-lotus posture with the right leg over the left, he displays the aspect of great loving-kindness and great compassion, adorned with jeweled garlands and celestial garments.
The kashaya is a wondrous necklace; rings and bracelets serve as armlets of jade.
A hundred blessings form the waist-cloth; the exquisite robes are the color of vermilion light.
A halo surrounds the entire body, with a precious lotus serving as the seat.
A jeweled crown adorns his head, in the center of which appears Amitāyus;
his dark blue hair falls over both shoulders.
Ten fully blossomed lotuses serve as his bracelets and anklets, while jade forms his arm-rings; a fine silk sash encircles his waist.
Clad in robes of deep crimson, his body adorned with the marks of compassion,
a halo of light pervades the world; his two feet rest upon precious lotuses,
a wondrous crown adorns his coiled hair, and his dark blue locks hang down by his ears.
The physical form is light purple; the left hand holds a sword upon a lotus of stability, while the right forms the fist of wisdom resting upon the knee.
With an expression of great compassion and pity, he wears a rosary, a monastic robe, celestial garments, and exquisite necklaces.
With bracelets and armlets of jade, and a waist-scarf of a thousand colors;
wearing a wondrous robe of crimson radiance, his body-light like that of a rainbow;
seated upon a precious lotus, he dwells peacefully within the ocean of the lunar disc.
Having already described the physical characteristics of the eight great bodhisattvas,
I shall now describe the images of the four great śrāvakas.
Outside the eight petals, in the four corners of the inner court, beginning from the northeast:
First is Mahākāśyapa; second, in the southeast, is Subhūti;
third, in the southwest, is Śāriputra.
In the fourth [direction], the northwest, the four great śrāvakas, Mahāmaudgalyāyana and the others, each have the appearance of a bhikṣu with a pale flesh-colored complexion.
Having thus described the physical characteristics of the four great śrāvakas,
I shall now describe the deportment, form, and color of the sixteen bodhisattvas in the second enclosure.
Wearing a sublime jewel crown upon his head, his body is the color of white flesh;
his left hand forms the mudrā of meditative concentration with the fist clenched, while his right hand holds a vajra-chain of wisdom.
His body is adorned with garlands and necklaces, and he sits in the full lotus posture with the right leg pressing upon the left.
Wearing a sublime jewel crown upon his head, his body is a deep blue color;
his left hand forms the mudrā of meditative concentration with a fist, while his right holds a wisdom vajra-bell.
Wearing a sublime jewel crown upon his head, his body is a deep black color.
The left hand is fixed in the fist-mudrā; the right hand holds a vajra-hook at the crown of the head.
He wears a sublime jewel-crown. His body is white-yellow in color;
the left hand holds a vajra-noose, and the right hand is clenched in a fist pressed against the knee.
Wearing a sublime jewel crown upon her head, her body is white-yellow in color;
holding a fresh flower with wisdom, she sits in the vajra-paryaṅka posture with the right leg pressing upon the left.
Wearing a sublime jewel crown upon her head, her body is a deep blue color.
The vessel for the ointment of meditative concentration and wisdom, as well as the body, are as described above;

upon the crown of the head is a sublime jewel tiara. The body is of a great black color, with the vessel for the incense of meditative concentration and wisdom; his bodily adornments are identical to those of Maitreya.
Wearing a sublime jewel crown upon his head, his body is of a great black color;
he holds an incense burner representing meditative concentration and wisdom,
as well as the five-hair crown mentioned above, within which the Vidyādhara dwells.
His body is fixed as a white lotus, flourishing yet not yet blossomed;

he is surrounded by a halo of light. His right hand displays the mudrā of preaching the Dharma, and his head is adorned with a crown of five locks of hair. The color of his body is that of white flesh.
The left hand forms the mudrā of preaching the Dharma; the right hand holds a great lotus upon which is a vajra.
He wears a crown of five topknots adorned with a crest-jewel and a garland of flames. His body is the color of white flesh.
In his left hand he firmly holds a great lotus, upon which are banners and streamers;
in his right hand of grace he holds a precious jewel.
He is encircled by a garland of flames and hundreds of thousands of varieties of necklaces, and his body is like that of Samantabhadra.
Wearing a crown of five top-knots, his body is reddish-yellow in color;
his left hand is in the mudrā of meditative concentration with the fist resting on the knee, while his right hand holds an alms-bowl atop a lotus of wisdom.
Wearing a crown of five top-knots, his body is lush yellow in color.
His left hand forms the *vajra-bandha* mudrā, while his right hand is in the *varada-muṣṭi* resting upon his knee.
He wears a crown of five topknots (*pañca-śikha*). His body is deep yellow in color;
in his upper left hand he holds a blue cloud and moon. He bestows ancient wisdom and fearlessness.
Wearing a crown of five topknots, his body is golden-yellow in color;
in his left hand he holds a vajra-wheel in the gesture of meditative concentration, and in his right hand he holds a lotus in the gesture of wisdom.
Wearing a crown of five topknots, his body is the color of white flesh.
On the left, the *Dinglian Shangjing*; on the right, the Huiquan pressing his knee;
these and the sixteen bodhisattvas above have their bodies adorned like Maitreya.
Having already described the majestic deportment and adorned bodies of each of the sixteen great bodhisattvas,
we now describe the ritual protocol for the third enclosure.
Their hair-tufts are adorned with jeweled crowns, and their faces are the color of fresh flesh.
With his left hand firmly grasping a sharp spear, his body is adorned with exquisite necklaces,
a *kāṣāya*, and celestial garments; he wears a vajra-jewel armor upon his right hip,
manifesting the majestic and wrathful aspect.
Seated in the full lotus posture with the right foot pressing upon the left, adorned with a crown of lotus petals and a topknot of hair; the face is the color of raw flesh;
the left hand in the mudrā of meditative concentration rests upon the knee, while the right hand holds a wisdom-vajra sword.
Adorned with a jeweled crown and a topknot, his face is white-yellow in color;
his left hand in the gesture of meditative concentration holds a jeweled stūpa, and his right hand in the gesture of wisdom holds a jeweled sword.
These four Great Heavenly Kings have majestic demeanors that adorn their bodies, identical to those of Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
His crown is adorned with a jeweled tiara, and he wears a three-pronged vajra upon his head.
His face is white-yellow in color; his left hand forms the mudrā of meditative concentration, while his right hand of wisdom holds a single-pronged vajra.
He is arrayed with hundreds of thousands of varieties of necklaces and ornaments.
Wearing a *kāṣāya* and flying celestial garments, she sits firmly upon a wondrous high throne.
She wears a crown of topknots on her head; her face is the color of white flesh, each face possessing three eyes. Her four hands hold flowers as marks of grace.
Next, for the mudrā of Bestowing and Holding the Rosary: With the hand of Samādhi above, hold the bell;
with the hand of Samādhi below, place the palm at the side.
Bend the ring finger while keeping the other nails straight, wearing exquisite necklaces, And a *kāṣāya* robe as well as celestial garments.
A circular halo conceals his jewel-like body;
he wears a sublime celestial crown upon his head. His face is like a purple lotus;
with wisdom and skillful means, he grasps a sharp spear, from which flows the water of the great black ox.
Adorned with exquisite jewel necklaces, celestial garments, and flying robes of subtle and wondrous colors,
he dwells atop the ocean of moon discs upon the head of a nine-headed nāga, whose body is the color of white flesh.
The left hand is fixed in the fist-mudrā; the right hand, in the gesture of grace, holds a noose with a wrathful expression for subduing.
Seated upon a lotus, she has the faces of a deer, a deer, and a horse; her body is the color of raw flesh.
Holding musical instruments, his body is naked in appearance with a horn crown upon his head;
his physical form is the color of raw flesh like that of a great bull-king, and in his left hand he firmly holds a flute.
To the right is Hweichih (Vajradhara), holding a precious sword and possessing the marks of great majestic power;
atop his head is a wish-fulfilling jewel. He has the head and beak of a bird with two wings, and his body is blue-black in color;
from his mouth he blows the conch, the chant, and the flute.
With a topknot crown upon his head, his body is dark blue-black in color;
his right hand forms the mudrā of wisdom of the asuras, while his face bears a wrathful expression.
His left hand holds a vajra-water vessel at the level of his navel, which is whirled like a wind-wheel above the void.
With his topknot encircling his own ground, his body is a great blue color,
adorned with vajra-jewel necklaces; possessing a most fierce expression,
he holds a noose in his left hand in the gesture of meditative concentration, while his right hand holds a rosary of jewels.

The right hand holds the three-pronged *triśūla*; the right hand forms the seal of Wisdom Fulfilling Vows, with the fingers of wisdom bent toward the vow-fingers; the power of wisdom is added directly to the mouth;
he wears a garment of animal skin; on his right side are two red snakes.
Coiled and entwined, they hang from the chest;
the face of the Principal Deity likewise has four arms, two of which are white.
A snake of a very pale blue-white color winds around it, as he dwells upon a lotus in a jeweled pond.
With a topknot and a crown of skulls, the color of dark clouds and lightning, possessing three eyes and a terrifying appearance; with eight arms wielding implements:
in the right hands, he holds a rosary, a vessel, and a golden wheel, while in the left hands, he holds a staff, a battle-axe, and a trident.
The left hand holds a vajra hook; the right hand of wisdom grasps three swords.
The right hand of wisdom forms a fist pressed against the side.
First, form the vajra-fist and extend the ring finger (śamkha-anguli) straight upward, positioned beneath the right side of the torso.
The Right Hand of Bestowing Fearlessness and the Seal of the Great Vow of Samādhi and Prajñā:
First, with the right hand of *prajñā*, press down upon the left hand of *samādhi*.
Curling the fingers into vajra-fists, the thumbs of both hands form the wind-wheels (*vāyu-maṇḍala*) of *samādhi* and *prajñā*.
Each stands upright against the chest; he wears a vajra-jewel necklace.
His eight left arms are encircled by eight snakes serving as beads, while two snakes wind around his two upper arms and two snakes wind around his two ears.
Clad in the skin of the king of beasts, with white lotuses supporting his two feet;
upon his topknot is an eight-petaled lotus. His topknot hangs over his left shoulder;
he has but one eye, gazing intently, with the features of his face like rippling waves.
The Great Wrathful One with White Fangs; in his left hand he holds a noose and a *kīla*, adorned with vajra-jewel necklaces and all manner of precious ornaments;
his majestic and wrathful body is garlanded with flames, and he stands upon a lion made of the seven jewels.
Wearing a crown of a great topknot of skulls, with the color of summer rain clouds,
having three faces each with three eyes, laughing "haṭṭa-haṭṭa" with an expression of extreme great wrath, he firmly holds a *khaṭvāṅga* in his left hand.
The left hand of method grasps the precious bow; the left hand of concentration holds the vajra-noose.
The right hand of wisdom wields the *vajra*; the right hand of wisdom holds the precious arrow.
This is the seal of the wisdom and method that saves the world; first, one stabilizes the left wrist with concentration.
Pressing upon the right *hita* (beneficent) wrist, cross the right *jñāna-bhūmi* (wisdom-ground) finger over the left *jñāna-bhūmi* finger like a suspended hook; likewise,
join the left *samādhi-pratipatti* (concentration-effort) water-finger with the *kṣānti-agni* (patience-fire) finger.

Bend the fingers so they enter the palm; likewise, with the wind-wheel of the precepts and the wheel of generosity, stand them upright, each attached to the other, with the head and arms like the two beaks of a bird;
the right hand of generosity is also like meditative concentration.
Adorned with a necklace of vajra-jewels, his sublime and wondrous body emits a radiance like crashing thunder and lightning; with a wreath of flames, there is none he does not illuminate.
Together with the consort Śambara, he takes their two bodies as his seat.
Having thus explained the three-tiered square altar,
the positions of the various deities,
as well as their postures, forms, and colors.
The shape of the mandala has already been explained.
Next, the ground of the inner court is the color of dark-blue lapis lazuli;
the ground of the second court is the color of red pearls.
The three enclosures are a light crimson color.
Between the inner enclosure and the second enclosure is ground of vaidūrya,
marked with the five-sword pattern.
From the second enclosure to the third gate is the ground of purple-gold lotuses,
marked with the three-pronged vajra pattern.
From the third enclosure to the Lotus Gate is the ground of red gold.
The text of the Solitary Sword:
next are the four square lotus gates, white-flesh colored, with vajra wooden stakes at the four corners in the form of a crossed *vajra*.
It is also called the *gandha* wooden stake.
The four cardinal directions and four intermediate corners were surrounded by blue lotuses.
Then, having spoken this sūtra, Bhagavān [the Blessed One] addressed the entire great assembly—
the maṇḍala of the Single Vehicle for the fulfillment of vows— and all the bodhisattvas, Vajrapāṇi, and the others.
Having heard what the Buddha had spoken,
their hearts were filled with great joy;
they believed, accepted, and practiced it accordingly.
Paid the blank contract copy.
